Hence, new approaches for the accurate diagnosis and treatment of cancer must be developed (Racioppi et al. Among numerous potential approaches available for cancer treatment, nanoparticle-based drug delivery exhibits better efficiency and selectivity than other conventional therapies and thus holds substantial potential.

Compared with nontargeted carriers, nanocarriers exhibited enhanced tumor internalization, diagnostic imaging, and prolonged survival in vivo (Large et al. However, tumor heterogeneity, scale-up problems, lack of adequate knowledge on influencing biological factors, and insufficient delivery at the target site still hinder the application of nanocarriers for cancer treatment.
A multifunctional theranostic approach for existing nanocarrier modalities has been increasingly used Vol.:(0112 334567 5 40 in recent years for cancer treatment.
Thus, a comprehensive review of different nanocarrier systems particularly focusing on newer theranostic multifunctional techniques is necessary.

Here, we review various nanocarrier-based approaches used to target tumors and their limitations, present clinical scenario, and future prospects with a particular focus on newer multifunctional designs and therapy.
Tumor cells and their environment Tumors progress in a complicated milieu required for their prolonged development, invasion, and metastasis.

Thus, a clear understanding of the tumor microenvironment (TME) and tumor progression mechanisms is essential for designing systems to target tumors (Fig. Diverse cellular and noncellular components form the TME, including neighboring blood vessels, immune cells, fibroblasts, cancer stem cells, and the extracellular matrix (ECM) (Ahn et al. Tumor cells obtain nutrients for their development through passive diffusion until they reach a size of approximately 2 mm3.
New blood vessels (angiogenesis) develop to ensure the adequate supply of nutrients to the expanding tumor mass.
Angiogenesis requires various biological signals for initiation.
However, because of irregularity in the process, tumors develop poorly vascularized areas with resultant necrosis and become more permeable.
This phenomenon occurs due to basement membrane deformities and a decrease in pericytes lining rapidly proliferating endothelial cells (Greish 20.

The variation in the aperture ranges from 100 to 800 nm between porous endothelial cells and from 5 to 10 nm between tight endothelial cells (Hobbs et al. In addition, the lack of well-defined lymphatic networks in tumors results in enhanced permeability and retention (EPR).
However, the tumor interstitium is made of a collagen matrix and a fluid (gel type) that results in high interstitial pressure, which causes resistance against the inflow of molecules.

Thus, drug transport through the tumor relies on the balance between the outward of different stages of tumour progression (Suijkerbuijk and Van 20 Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 52:539–585 interstitial pressure and various factors including drug particle size, hydrophobic nature, and electrical charge.
Accelerated proliferation in tumor cells along with a deficient vasculature often results in dynamic tumor hypoxia.

The TME has a lower pH than do physiological tissues because of excess lactic acid formation and altered tumor cell metabolism, also known as the Warburg effect (Fais et al. 20, and such microenvironment drives tumor progression and development (Feuerecker et al. Tumor hypoxia and pH have been employed in various cancer treatments, particularly for the advancement of nanoformulations to improve the delivery of anticancer drugs.
The ECM is another potential component that can be exploited for targeting tumors.

The ECM is typically made of the basement membrane and interstitial matrix, contributing to tissue building and controlling cell expansion and relocation (Lu et al. 20; the ECM is strictly regulated in healthy tissues.
However, in tumors, ECM dysregulation occurs because of atypical enzyme expression, which leads to the accelerated dysregulation of the ECM and the degradation of the basement membrane.
All these factors hinder drug delivery to tumors.
The complexity of the TME leads to an early decline in the drug delivery system, circulation time, and target cell uptake.

However, the TME can be exploited using nanotechnology-based approaches for the targeted delivery of anticancer drugs (Bennie et al. The lack of sufficient delivery to the target site is another factor that affects treatment efficacy; thus, a suitable targeting strategy is essential.

Targeting options for the delivery of nanoparticles to the TME EPR‑based drug delivery Diffusion in tumors decreases at a tumor volume of ≥ 2 mm3, causing a reduction in nutrition input, waste excretion, and Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 52:539–585 oxygen delivery (Hanahan and Weinberg 20.
Thus, the tumor tends to generate tumor-associated neurovasculature due to angiogenesis.

Angiogenesis is regulated by various angiogenic signaling molecules (both pro and anti), including vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), plateletderived growth factor, angiopoietins, and thrombospondins (Bergers and Benjamin 20.

Accelerated proliferation and vascularization leads to the formation of deformed and incomplete tumor vasculature with leaky vessels (Kalyane et al. 2019; Kutova et al. In addition, an irregular basement membrane is formed due to deficient pericytic and smooth muscle cells, which impair the drainage capacity (Fig. The defective tumor endothelium lacks this response to inflammatory stimuli.

The activation of the endothelium by angiogenic factors results in the formation of a defective basement membrane and irregularity in the structure, leading to increased vascular leakage and retention (also known as EPR) (Suijkerbuijk and Van 20.
De Sanctis et al. 2018 reported that this phenomenon complicates the TME, causing it to become immunosuppressive.
EPR is a physiology-based primary mechanism of the agglomeration of large molecules and small particles in tumors.

The EPR property has been successfully used to cure different types of cancer and its use is considered the first generation of passively targeted nanomedicine (Kutova et al. 2019; Prabhakar et al. Passive targeting using EPR has been extensively described by Byrne et al (20 in their review on the active targeting schemes of nanocarriers and by Klein (20 in their study on the importance of the tics of normal versus tumorassociated endothelium (Klein et al. 20 tumor vascular endothelium in cancer treatment (Byrne et al. 2008; Klein 20.

Recent studies on EPR‑based nanomedicine In this section, we discuss some of the recent studies on first-generation tumor targeting based on the EPR effect. 2017 reported that albumin-bound paclitaxel SN-38-encapsulated nanoporphyrin micelles (SN-NPM) enhanced antitumor activity in vitro in colon cancer cells by 78- and 350-fold in a single therapy.

They prepared small-sized SN-NPM that had longer tumor holding time (> 5 days) and caused substantial agglomeration in tumors (Yang et al. In a similar study, Mo et al. (20 prepared three sorafenib-encapsulated liposomal formulations, namely uncoated, hyaluronic acid–coated, and polyethylene glycol (PEG)ylated hyaluronic acid–coated liposomes, with small size distribution and increased encapsulation efficiency for breast cancer therapy based on EPR. They indicated that PEGylated hyaluronic acid–coated liposomes were the most effective in inhibiting tumor growth and had enhanced systemic exposure and longer blood circulation (Mo et al. Moreover, such enhanced retention was reported by other studies using PEG-modified croconaine dye (CR7 (Tang et al. 20, doxorubicin-loaded magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles for brain tumor treatment (Lee et al. 20, and folic acid-decorated polyamidoamine dendrimer G4 (G4-FA) for the local delivery of siRNA in head and neck carcinoma (Xu et al. The major limitation of EPR-based passive targeting using nanomedicine is the inconsistency in outcomes due 5 42 to the heterogeneity of many complex biological processes including differences in cancer genetics (Bertrand et al. Golombek et al. (20 reported wide interand intra-individual heterogeneity in tumor targeting based on EPR. They suggested the need to move toward improved individualized nanomedicine treatment unlike the current one-size-fits-all tumor targeting approach.

The nature, complexity, and heterogeneity of the EPR effect should be determined and new systems and designs for EPR-based tumor targeting should be developed (Golombek et al. Klein (20 highlighted a different aspect of EPR and indicated that EPR might reduce the treatment response because it causes an imbalance in areas with oversupply or undersupply of intravenous drugs in cancer therapy.

Furthermore, they suggested developing tumor vasculature–targeting agents that specifically target tumor endothelial cells to improve the potency of currently used cancer therapies, especially immunotherapies (Klein 20. 20 recommended various pharmacological and physical strategies to increase the tumor accumulation and potency of EPR-based nanomedicines.
Among them, the most crucial are drugs regulating VEGF signaling, angiotensin agonists and antagonists, TNF-α agents, vessel-stimulating therapies, and nitric oxideproducing agents.

In addition, hyperthermia, radiotherapy, and ultrasound have been utilized in recent years in various theranostic designs (Nel et al. Because the heterogeneity of EPR in different tumors causes complications in developing a clinically successful design, studies have attempted to employ other tumor-targeting strategies.
We believe that the insufficient delivery of a drug in the tumor region due to the lack of specificity and guided delivery is a major limitation of passive targeting.
However, passive targeting based on the EPR effect remains the most clinically successful nanosystem for tumor targeting.

Ligand‑mediated targeted NP or nanoconjugates The major limitation of passive targeting is that small drug molecules are not retained and leak out due to the absence of specific binding to cellular proteins after they penetrate the tumor interstitial space.
Thus, ligand-mediated active binding of nanocarriers to overexpressed receptors present on tumor cells is considered an effective means of drug targeting.

These overexpressed receptors are favorable potential sites for the ligand-mediated active targeting of anticancer drugs, and the second generation of nanomedicines targeting specific tumors have been developed using this approach.

Specific ligands exhibiting an affinity for a particular receptor are attached to the surface of nanocarriers, leading to favorable binding and uptake at the action site (Akhtar et al. 2014, Ramzy et al. Figure 3 summarizes the common receptor overexpression associated with each different type Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 52:539–585 of cancer.

Many studies have focused on different ligands and receptors, such as the folate receptor (Amreddy et al. 2018; Raniolo et al. 20, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) (Venugopal et al. 2018; Yan et al. 20, monoclonal antibodies (Miller et al. 2016; Hellmann et al. 20, hyaluronic-based CD44 targeting (Rosa et al. 2017; Wickens et al. 20, transferrin (Jhaveri et al. 2018; Choudhury et al. 20, and peptide-mediated targeting (Yeh et al. 2016; Bashari et al. 2017; Gilad et al. These studies have demonstrated that ligand-mediated targeting significantly improved the site-specific cellular uptake and anticancer efficacy compared with passive targeting.
However, rapid clearance from systemic circulation is a concern due to uptake by the mononuclear phagocytic system.
In addition, this problem is encountered during the development of stealth nanocarriers by using hydrophilic polymers or surfactants that reduce their opsonization (Rizvi and Saleh 20.

Antibody‑based targeting ligands Antibody-based targeting ligands are the most extensively used as potential drug carriers because of their distinct in vivo characteristics and enhanced target specificity.

Antibodies and their derived fragments were used as targeting ligands for nanoparticulate therapeutics and diagnostic tools for cancer therapy (Richards et al. High immunogenicity, low efficacy due to poor drug loading, and poor stability are major drawbacks limiting the use of whole antibodies.
The majority of these problems have been solved by the use of antibody fragments that have low immunogenicity, higher drug loading, and improved efficacy.

Moreover, advances in protein engineering, particularly phage display techniques, have led to the development of many new antibody fragments (nanobodies; e.g., ScFv, ds-Fv, ds-ScFv, single-domain antibodies [sdAbs], and diabodies) (Dmitriev et al. scFv is the most widely used fragment.

A study used scFv in conjugation with the p53 DNA plasmid targeting receptor transferrin (Senzer et al. In another similar study, scFv was used in conjugation with trastumazb for targeting HER2 in liposomal formulation (Miller et al. In a recent study, anti-CEA MFE23-scFv-based N-terminal trimer bodies were prepared and combined with PET for theranostic use in gastric cancer (Rios et al. sdAbs are the smallest fragments that maintain the maximum antigen-binding capacity of antibodies with favorable characteristics similar to drugs and were extensively reviewed by Iezzi et al. (20. sdAbs are mostly engineered from the variable heavy-chain fragment (VHH gene) present in Camelidae heavy-chain antibodies (or IgG2 and IgG. These antibodies bind to the hepatocyte growth factor, EGFR, bone morphogenetic protein (TGF-β superfamily Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 52:539–585 expression associated with each different types of cancer. (Large et al. 20 growth factors), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER, cMET, or VEGFR1 and can prevent tumor cell proliferation.

HER2, EGFR, transferrin receptor (TfR), and prostatespecific membrane antigen are among the most extensively investigated mAb-mediated targets (Bazak et al. The Food and Drug Administration has approved several mAb therapies, and numerous clinical trials are ongoing (Hare et al. However, several factor limitation the use of mAbs.
Firer and Gellerman (20 summarized these limitations in their review.

Discovery of new cell surface targets, use of generation technology, molecular structures, intracellular transport, suboptimal pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics, antigenicity of the final product, tumor penetration, manufacture, and quality control are some of the major problems associated with antibody-mediated targeting.
Some of these limitations may be overcome with newer developments in peptide studies (Firer and Gellerman 20.
Peptide‑based targeting Numerous molecular targets for peptides exist on both cancer vasculature and cancer cells.
Peptides are classified into three groups: integrins, growth factor receptors (GFRs), and G-protein coupled receptors.

Peptide-based active receptor targeting has some major advantages, including structural design possibilities, decreased immunogenicity, and enhanced internalization (Accardo et al. Some of the recent studies on peptide-based active targeting have been discussed below.
Yeh et al. (20 used liposomal doxorubicin and vinorelbine conjugated with targeting peptides for prostate cancer.
By using phage display as a new peptide, they identified that SP204 can bind to prostate cancer cells.

The biodistribution profiles of drugs in peptide-coupled superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) and liposomes in tumors and normal organs were examined and compared with those of nontargeting drugs, and the peptide SP204 was determined to have significant potential for targeting prostate cancer (Yeh et al. The conjugation of targeting peptides with imaging contrast agents, such as quantum dots (QDs) and SPIONs, have led to the specific delivery of these agents to tumor sites. 2017 used 7mer peptides with a phage library to study targeted multi-rug delivery to prostate cancer cells.

The peptide (P, which was determined to precisely target PC-3 tumors in vivo, was included in monodrug (chlorambucil, 5 44 combretastatin, or camptothecin) and dual-drug (chlorambucil/combretastatin or chlorambucil/camptothecin) peptide–drug conjugates (PDCs), and the cytotoxic potential of these conjugates for target cells was determined.

Conjugation of P12 into dual-drug PDCs led to the discovery of new drug combinations with synergistic effects (Bashari et al. Similar approaches have been used to determine the efficacy of the LFC131 peptide (Wang et al. 2015a, b) and (EGFRAb) (Sundarraj et al. 20 for lung cancer.
Different strategies are employed for the peptide-based targeted delivery of chemotherapeutics to overexpressed receptors.
Phage display library, synthetic peptide library, SPOT synthesis, and rational designing are some of the widely used techniques.

A recent study described the targeted delivery of chemotherapeutics based on clinically studies peptides, including arginine–glycine–aspartic acid (RGD) (Cui et al. 20, somatostatin, luteinizing hormonereleasing hormone, and bombesin, was reported (Wang et al. A study provided extensive insights into various approaches based on these systems (Gilad et al. Currently, PDCs are an emerging class of prodrugs prepared using a specific peptide sequence covalently attached to a drug through a cleavable linker and are being used for actively targeting specific receptors on tumor cells (Wang et al. This approach will be discussed later in the section on prodrug-based targeting.
Multifunctional approaches have been recently used in peptide-based targeting due to their theranostic properties.

Aptamer‑based nanocarriers Aptamers are short single-stranded oligonucleotides or peptides possessing distinct three-dimensional structures with lower immunogenicity and stronger tissue penetration capacity compared with those of therapeutic antibodies.

These systems have resulted in more favorable uptake by tumor cells while minimizing unwanted side effects on healthy tissues (Esposito et al. In recent years, aptamer-based targeting has been employed in theranostic approaches.
Recently, Vandghanooni et al. (20 conducted a detailed review on such aptamer-based multimodal theranostic nanosystems for imaging and targeted cancer therapy.

They indicated that these short aptamers can be a better alternative to antibodies because of their smaller sizes that that of mAbs and Ab fragments; moreover, short aptamers are more capable of identifying protein epitopes that an Ab might fail to access (Vandghanooni et al. 20 and have higher penetrability into target cells.

Aptamers can be produced using an in vitro chemical combinatorial method called the systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) used for organ/tissue-specific Aps selection in vivo, unlike the production of mAbs, which is tedious Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 52:539–585 and often fails to have high affinity.
SELEX can be help in choosing a wide range of targets from small to biomacromolecules.
The Biomarker SELEX method has been beneficial in the development of several aptamer-based cancer targeting strategies (Dua et al. 2013; Zhou et al 20.
Furthermore, unlike Abs, aptamers exhibit considerable capability for chemical modification beyond the loss of function to enhance their stability and blood halflife.
In addition, they are nontoxic and nonimmunogenic.
These systems are beneficial when used in combination with drug-carrying nanomaterials or siRNAs for enhancing the therapeutic response of anticancer agents.

This aptamer-based system has been used for treating various cancers such as pancreatic (Kratschmer and Ley 20, breast (Jalalian et al. 20, brain (Esposito et al 2018a, b), lung (Ayatollahia et al. 20, hepatic (Ladju et al. 2018; Trinh et al. 20, and lymphoma (Parekh et al. Hori et al. (20 performed an extensive review on current advances in aptamers for cancer diagnosis and therapy and discussed the development of aptamers and related challenges encountered in the last 5 years for cancer diagnosis and therapy.
The high-throughput selection process used for identifying high-affinity target-specific aptamers can help reduce the time required for the isolation of aptamers in the near future.
Although only two aptamer-based cancer therapeutics reached the clinical trial stage, many aptamers have exhibited substantial capability for targeted cancer therapy.
The use of covalent or noncovalent conjugation strategies has been beneficial for many aptamers because they act building blocks for functionalizing other therapeutic agents.
This property would expedite their clinical translation.
In addition to the theranostic approach, immunotherapy is another potential approach.

A multispecific nucleic acid aptamer-based immunotherapeutic modality is being widely used for maintaining cancerspecific immunity for tumor cell removal (Hori et al. Some practical limitations should be addressed to enhance aptamer use in cancer treatment in the future, including the high cost of modified oligonucleotides and instability in vivo resulting from nuclease-mediated deterioration and rapid renal filtration.
Folate targeting The FR is among the most widely studied receptors that are overexpressed in most common tumors (e.g., ovarian, lung, brain, and colorectal cancer).
The FR is a glycoprotein existing in two isoforms, namely FR-α and FR-β.

Folic acid can serve as an effective ligand targeting these receptors (Narmani et al. Folate-based nanocarriers are less toxic because folic acid is a vitamin and demonstrated satisfactory stability to pH changes and heat.

Moreover, folic acid exhibits a high potential for scaling up. Folate-based Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 52:539–585 nanocarriers have been extensively used in lung cancer (Amreddy et al. 2018; Tan and Wang 20, ovarian cancer (Chen et al. 20, cervical cancer/adenocarcinoma (Raniolo et al. 20, breast cancer (Wu et al. 2018a, b, c), glioblastoma (Minaei et al. 20, and liver cancer (Koirala et al. Folate-based carriers have been the most explored among ligand-based active targeting agents.

Recent studies have combined these folate-based nanocarriers with suitable contrast agents for the imaging and designing of new theranostic agents for cancer therapy (Qin et al. Transferrin modification The TfR is a glycoprotein of the cell membrane and is involved in regulating the growth of cells and the cellular uptake of transferrin.
Transferrin and transferrin-binding antibodies are major ligands involved in receptor-mediated endocytosis.

Shen et al. (2018a, b) conducted a detailed review on transferrin-mediated tumor targeting (Shen et al. The TfRs are 100 times more expressed on tumor cells than on normal cells (Danhier et al. Thus, the TfR is among the most explored overexpressed receptors for targeted delivery, and few nanoconjugates are in clinical studies (Van der Meel et al. Different types of nanocarriers have been developed for TfR-mediated site-specific delivery, including polymeric nanoparticles, metallic nanoparticles, niosomes, liposomes, and lipid nanocarriers (Yameen et al. 20, for different types of cancers, such as lung (Xu et al. 2018a, b; Li et al. 2017a, b, c), colorectal (Moghimipour et al. 20, and brain (Jhaveri et al. Despite the considerable research on active targeting using different ligands, the translational success in the clinical phase is still not encouraging.
The designed nanocarriers using different ligands still failed to achieve adequate sitespecific delivery clinically due to various biological barriers.

Hence, in an extensive review, Large et al. (20 reported that to develop an optimized drug delivery system for ligand-mediated targeting, high-throughput screening must be performed during the development phase itself.

Such an approach can successfully reduce the time and cost required to identify the most effective delivery system (Large et al. Moreover, the combination of these approaches with suitable image-guided agents and therapy would lead to the development of multifunctional systems as potential alternatives, and present works are mostly headed in that direction.
Stimuli‑responsive methods The active targeting designs are limited by numerous biological barriers that result in insufficient delivery.

These barriers include biodistribution, immune activation, blood circulation, tumor target agglomeration, tumor tissue perforation, tumor cell internalization, and release (Fig. 4) (Wang et al. This has led to the development of an efficient strategy considering all these processes to ensure efficient site-specific delivery to tumors.

Various exogenous and endogenous stimuli-responsive systems have been developed for effective delivery (Hossen et al. 2018; Wu et al. However, in recent years, most of these approaches are used in combination with ligand-mediated systems and suitable imaging modalities for designing multifunctional theranostic nanocarriers.

Exogenous systems Thermosensitive nanocarriers Mild hyperthermia has been recently used as an effective strategy for anticancer drug delivery due to its cytotoxicity at temperatures of 40–42 °C and its ability to sensitize tumor cells to chemotherapy.

Thermo-responsive nanocarrier systems have been designed using materials that can protect the drug until it reaches the tumor site and is safe and susceptible to temperature changes between 39 and 42 °C, where hyperthermia causes carrier extravasation and on-site triggered release.

Redox‑responsive nanocarriers Redox-responsive nanocarriers are stimuli-responsive formulations used for drug targeting and respond to physiological signals.

These nanocarriers are based on disulfide cleavable crosslinkers and are developed to degrade in the physiologically reducing environment and expedite the release of loaded drugs (Puri et al. The disulfide linker is reduction sensitive and is easily broken down by elevated GSH concentrations.
GSH is a tripeptide made of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine and contains abundant thiol species in the cytoplasm.
GSH is a crucial reducing ligand in biochemical processes.
GSH/ glutathione disulfide (GSSG) is abundant in the cytoplasm (1–10 µM), although its concentration reduces to approximately 2–20 µM outside of cells.
Moreover, the GSH level in tumor tissues are four times higher than those in the normal tissue.
Thus, this redox potential difference has been considered to design nanocarriers for achieving the site-specific delivery of anticancer drugs (Ghorbani and Hamishehkar 20.

Enzyme‑mediated delivery Alterations in the manifestation of certain enzymes in tumors can be employed for targeting the TME. Various enzymes belonging to protease and lipase families exhibited by cancer cells can be used as endogenous triggers for cancer imaging and therapy (Senapati et al. Newer multifunctional theranostic designs Utilization of theranostic designs for developing integrated cancer cell diagnostics and therapy has been among of the most significant advancements in nanocarriers.
Molecular imaging devices are capable of characterizing biological processes at cellular and subcellular levels.
With the use of appropriate contrast agents, molecular imaging can aid in the early identification of cancer growth, improved comprehension, and image-guided drug delivery at the target site.

Optical imaging (bioluminescence and fluorescence), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), nuclear imaging (positron emission tomography [PET] and single-photon emission computerized tomography [SPECT]), and ultrasound are the most commonly employed technologies.
These systems are gradually being integrated with other active targeting techniques or stimuli-responsive approaches, resulting in a more multifunctional targeting approach.
Several multifunctional nanosystems involving the use of molecular imaging with contrast agents, either alone or in combination with chemotherapeutic medication, are being developed.

These multifunctional systems are developed by combining them with appropriate ligands for ligand-mediated targeted delivery or stimuli-responsive agents (pH, 5 60 temperature, and ultrasound) for stimuli-responsive targeted drug release.

Different nanocarriers have been successfully constructed for this multifunctional theranostic method, and these systems have recently been employed to combine chemotherapy, photothermal therapy, photodynamic therapy (PDT), and photoacoustic therapy, with promising results.
Optical imaging is among the most commonly utilized imaging modalities.
Optical imaging involved the use of photons released by bioluminescence or fluorescent sources.
The main benefits of the method are its low cost, safety, and excellent spatial resolution in visible and near-infrared fluorescence (NIRF) spectra.
However, it has limitations in fluorescence imaging in the visible range of 395–600 nm due to its limited penetration (0–2 cm) and high susceptibility to disturbances.
Moreover, the results of this method are affected by tissue autofluorescence and protein absorption (257–280 nm), heme groups (maximum at 560 nm), and water absorption (above 900 nm).
These drawbacks can be overcome by operating the system in the near-infrared range (700–900 nm), which is the most commonly employed in this approach.

Clinical scenario and approved products The use of targeted nanomedicines has been explored and is developing with innovations and advancements in interdisciplinary research.

Despite the problems of scaling up, formulations, lack of suitable characterization methods, stability, toxicity, and regulatory obligations, the number of targeted nanomedicines approved and used in clinical studies is increasing.
Six liposomal formulations, two polymer–protein conjugates, one polymeric nanoparticle, one polymeric micelle, and one magnetic nanoparticle are currently available in the market (Table 9).
The first generation of anticancer nanocarriers to be approved by the FDA included liposomes and polymeric conjugates.

Doxil (liposomal DOX) was the first anticancer nanomedicine to be approved by the FDA in 1995, and Onivyde (PEG-stealth liposome) is the newest one to be approved in 2015 for the passive targeting of irinotecan in pancreatic cancer.

Among polymeric nanoparticles, Eligard is the only approved PLGA-based nanocarrier for passive targeting of leuprolide acetate through subcutaneous injection in advanced prostate cancer.

Expert comments In the recent decade, the field of nanocarriers for cancertargeted delivery has advanced significantly.
The first anticancer nanocarrier used passive targeting based on the EPR effect in tumors.
This method is used in the majority of approved nanoformulations and clinical trials for cancer targeting.
Polymeric conjugates, polymeric nanoparticles, and polymeric micelles are among the most successful nanocarriers.
The lack of site specificity as well as the problems of retention and clearance are the primary limitations of the first-generation cancer targeting approaches.

Thus, there has been a surge in ligand-mediated active targeting, also known as second-generation cancer targeting, which is focused on employing various ligands to target overexpressed receptors on various cancers.
Numerous studies based on folate receptor, epidermal growth factor receptor, monoclonal antibody, hyaluronic acid, transferrin, peptide-mediated, and other factors have been conducted in this area.
Many studies have focused on aptamers and siRNA-based active targeting for various malignancies.
Compared with passive targeting, ligand-mediated treatments have demonstrated significant improvements in sitespecific cellular uptake and anticancer activity.

Despite all improvements, active targeting approaches are yet to succeed clinically in achieving sufficient site-specific delivery, and the biological barriers remain the major hindrance.

Furthermore, cancer cells are positioned proximal to the endothelial barrier in fast-developing tumors, and nanocarriers containing targeting moieties would attach to the first receptors they detect instead of penetrating the remaining tumor.
An additional disadvantage of active targeting nanocarriers that contributes to their present clinical failure is their higher immunogenicity when targeting moieties are added to the nanocarriers.

Immunotherapy is another crucial treatment option for cancer, and researchers are attempting to create nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems that might boost immunotherapy and reeducate the immunosuppressive TME. Tumor macrophages, nano vaccines, artificial antigen-presenting cells, nanoparticles reversing tumor immunosuppressive milieu, and checkpoint inhibition are some nanoparticlebased specialized immunotherapeutic methods that have been investigated.

Multiple failures have been encountered in the successful use of the treatment for patients, with the main barriers being poor scale-up, lack of appropriate characterization methods, stability, toxicity, and regulatory obligations.
The absence of data on the scaling-up of nanoformulations obstructs their commercialization even further.

Although some success in the clinical trials of nanocarrier designs based on active targeting has been observed, the main reasons for failure are the lack of understanding of disease heterogeneity in the patient community and physiological barriers such as tumor penetration, hypoxia, and endosomal escape as well as the failure to provide sufficient evidence supporting a specific end. For greater success, we must first gain a deeper understanding of various clinical tumors and factors that affect the clinical performance of these nanomedicines.

Nanoparticle preparation processes must be simplified, with good industrial scaleup validation and batch-to-batch consistency.
Tumor heterogeneity and biological limitations to tumor targeting continue to be key roadblocks.

Given the various obstacles that prevent the drug from reaching the site of action in sufficient amounts, a combination method must be designed to overcome these obstacles by using various approaches.

Thus, the recent development of a multifunctional method incorporating multiple approaches, such as stimuli-responsive targeting, ligand-mediated targeting, and passive nanocarrier behavior combined with theranostic designs, or immunotherapeutic approach appears to be the most promising.

Most of these techniques, which adopt a theranostic approach and are multifunctional, involving appropriate imaging modalities (optical imaging, MRI, ultrasound, SPECT, and PET) as well as chemotherapy in combination with various passive or active targeting, have demonstrated promising results in overcoming various biological barriers that affect tumor targeting.

Currently, these multifunctional theranostic designs combine chemotherapy with photodynamic or photothermal therapy and show high potential for developing more efficient anti-cancer targeting systems with high specificity, lower toxicity, resistance, and recurrence.

To overcome the various limitations of cancer targeting and therapy, a multifunctional approach based on a combination of ligand-mediated targeting, stimuli-responsive targeting, immunotherapeutic methods, and theranostic designs using nanocarriers is a potential system that must be investigated.

Conclusion Nanomedicines have demonstrated their capacity to overcome the limitations of poor pharmacokinetics and biopharmaceutical distribution, nonspecific cytotoxicity, and optimal bioavailability for cancer treatment.

The multifunctional approach using nanocarriers based on a combination of ligand-mediated targeting, stimuli-responsive targeting, immunotherapeutic methods, and theranostic designs can be potential systems that can solve the various limitations of cancer targeting and therapy.
However, for the bench-to-bedside translation of nanomedicines for cancer therapy, future studies evaluating their safety, efficacy, scale-up potential, and regulatory compliance are warranted.
